They are so small we barely notice them, and yet they are, in one way, the true rulers of the earth. For every single person alive, there are more than a billion insects. They were here long before us, they are everywhere around us, and life as we know it could not go on without them. This is the story of the smallest and mightiest animals of all.

image.note: A swarm of many different insects

pages.text: Insects are the most numerous animals on earth, of more kinds than all other animals put together. Beetles, ants, bees, flies, butterflies, and thousands upon thousands more: a whole vast kingdom of tiny creatures, living quiet, busy, astonishing lives just beneath our notice.

image.note: A dazzling variety of insects together

pages.text: How many insects are there? More than anyone can count. Scientists believe there may be millions of different kinds, and most have not even been named yet. In a single handful of soil, or the branches of one tree, there may be more insects than there are people in a large town.

image.note: Countless insects in a single patch of earth

pages.text: They live nearly everywhere: in deserts and forests, in ponds and puddles, high on mountains and deep in the soil, in your garden and even in your home. They have found a way to live in almost every corner of the world. Wherever you go, the insects were there first.

image.note: Insects thriving in many different places

pages.text: With so many kinds, how do you know an insect when you see one? Every true insect shares the same plan. Its body comes in three parts: a head, a middle, and a back part. It has six legs, always six, never more, never fewer. And most have a pair of feelers, and many have wings.

image.note: An insect's body labelled: three parts, six legs, feelers

pages.text: So a spider, with its eight legs and two body parts, is not an insect at all, though people often think it is. Nor is a worm, or a snail. The six legs are the great test. Count the legs, and you will know a true insect from all its small crawling cousins.

image.note: An insect beside a spider, legs counted

pages.text: Insects have no bones inside them, as we do. Instead they wear their skeleton on the outside, a hard shell that holds them together and protects them, like a suit of armour. It is one reason they can be so tough for their size, and why a beetle can carry many times its own weight.

image.note: An insect's hard outer shell, like armour

pages.text: Many insects do something truly astonishing as they grow: they change their shape completely. A butterfly does not begin as a butterfly at all. It begins as an egg, which hatches into a caterpillar, a soft, hungry, crawling thing that does nothing but eat and grow.

image.note: An egg hatching into a caterpillar

pages.text: Then, when it is fully grown, the caterpillar does an extraordinary thing. It wraps itself in a case, and inside, hidden away, its whole body is remade. After a time the case splits open, and out climbs not a caterpillar at all, but a butterfly, with wings, ready to fly. It is one of the true marvels of nature.

image.note: A caterpillar becoming a butterfly inside its case

pages.text: Some insects live alone, but others live together in vast numbers, in colonies of thousands, working as one. Ants build great underground cities, with rooms and tunnels and stores. Some ants even keep gardens, or herd smaller insects for their sweet juice, farming, in their own tiny way.

Bees, too, live in busy cities of their own, and do a wonderful thing: they dance. When a bee finds flowers, it returns to the hive and dances a special pattern that tells the others exactly where to fly. With a little dance, one bee sends a thousand others straight to the food.

image.note: A bee dancing to show others where flowers are

pages.text: It would be easy to think we could do without insects. Nothing could be further from the truth. Insects are among the most important animals on earth, and if they vanished, our whole world would fall apart. They do quiet, vital work that almost nothing else can do.

image.note: Insects at their vital work in nature

pages.text: Most important of all, insects carry the dust that lets flowers make seeds and fruit. As a bee moves from flower to flower for its food, it carries this dust with it, and without that, countless plants could not grow, and much of the food we eat would simply disappear. We owe our very dinners to the insects.

image.note: A bee carrying pollen between flowers

pages.text: So the next time you see an insect, a beetle trundling, a butterfly drifting, an ant hurrying with a crumb, do not brush it aside. Look closer. You are looking at one of the most successful, ancient, and important animals on earth, going quietly about the work that keeps our whole living world turning.

image.note: A child looking closely and kindly at an insect

pages.text: They are small, and they are countless, and they are easy to miss. But the little rulers were here before us, and they hold the living world together in a thousand quiet ways. The mightiest kingdom on earth is also the smallest, buzzing and crawling all around you, right now.

image.note: The vast, busy world of insects all around

pages.text: Words to know. Insect: a small animal with three body parts and six legs. Colony: a great group of insects living together. Caterpillar: the young, crawling stage of a butterfly or moth. Pollen: the dust insects carry that lets plants make seeds. Antennae: an insect's feelers.
Insects are the smallest rulers of the land. But other cold-blooded creatures share the world too, scaled and sunbathing, from the tiny lizard to the great crocodile. Which will you meet next?
